_doc: Jitter buffer vectors, PROTOCOL.md "Voice". Each case runs a fresh buffer against a virtual millisecond clock: process the steps in file order, setting the clock to `at` first (non-decreasing). insert = [seq, ts] of an audio packet arriving (payload irrelevant: packets are identified by seq); keepalive = seq of a keepalive arriving; pull = one 20 ms frame is due, with the expected result: "play <seq>", "fec <seq>" (the lost frame is decoded from the FEC copy in the successor packet <seq>, which stays queued), "conceal" (PLC) or "silence". expect = counters that must hold at that point, any subset of targetMs / underruns (packets that arrived after their slot) / shed (queued frames dropped by the backlog rules or the 400 ms hard cap). Constants the cases rely on: target 40..200 ms in 20 ms steps, lowered after 10 s without an underrun; a spurt starts once its oldest queued packet has waited the target; 'last played frame' for the late-first-packet rule is the last frame returned as play; at most 3 conceals on an empty queue, then silence; a late run of 100 ms with nothing played re-anchors (new spurt at the next late packet, earlier queue dropped); a ts more than 3 s from the playout clock restarts the buffer; shed frames set the last-seen seq and the playout clock as if they had played. Generated from the Android implementation (core/JitterBuffer.kt); the _why of a case is a comment.

cases.name: steady stream
cases._why: One packet per 20 ms, 5 ms of network delay: the first plays 40 ms after it arrived and nothing is ever shed.

cases.name: burst at spurt start
cases._why: Five packets arrive together (the radio woke up), then the stream is steady: only the target's worth of the burst is kept, so the spurt starts at the target depth and not 80 ms deeper.

cases.name: reordered burst within the target
cases._why: Three packets arrive together out of order: they span exactly the target, none is shed, they play in ts order.

cases.name: playout stall 700 ms
cases._why: Pulls stop for 700 ms mid-spurt (route switch, blocked write) while packets keep arriving. The first pull after it applies the 400 ms hard cap; the next 1 s window ends with its smallest depth far above the target and the whole excess is dropped at once, so the depth is back at the target about 1 s after the stall.

cases.name: output clock 1 % slow
cases._why: A frame is due every 20.2 ms (pull times rounded to the ms) against a 20 ms sender for 30 s: the depth creeps up until a window's smallest depth exceeds target + 40 ms, then one frame is shed per window, about every 2 s, and the depth never runs away.

cases.name: output clock 5 % slow
cases._why: A frame is due every 21 ms for 12 s: one frame per window is not enough, so the depth keeps growing until a window's smallest depth exceeds target + 120 ms and the whole excess goes at once; then it repeats.

cases.name: underrun raises the target once per spurt
cases._why: Seq 10 and seq 20 each arrive after their slot in the same spurt (a conceal is heard in the slot): two underruns, one 20 ms raise. The raise applies from the next spurt (after a silence gap with a keepalive), where a third late packet raises it again.

cases.name: target lowers after 10 s
cases._why: One late packet raises the target to 60 ms; 10 s without another lowers it to 40 ms again, and it never goes below 40. The running spurt keeps its timing throughout.

cases.name: loss: FEC and concealment
cases._why: Seq 5 is lost with its successor queued when it is due: FEC from seq 6. Seqs 10 and 11 are lost: the first has no immediate successor (conceal), the second is decoded from seq 12. Loss is not an underrun.

cases.name: silence gap starts a new spurt
cases._why: The sender goes quiet (DTX) after seq 9: at most 3 conceals, then silence. Two keepalives fill seqs 10 and 11. Seq 12 has a ts 50 frames on: contiguous seq, so it is not loss but a new spurt that plays a target after it arrived, with no FEC or concealment for the gap. The second gap has no keepalive at all (shorter than 1 s).

cases.name: new spurt's first packet arrives late
cases._why: After a 600 ms silence gap the network delay is 100 ms more than before, so the old spurt's playout clock has passed the new packet's slot when it arrives. Nothing is queued, the ts jumped and only a keepalive lies between: a new spurt, not an underrun, and no frame is lost.

cases.name: bunched late arrival after a pause
cases._why: Same, but the first 11 frames of the new utterance arrive in one bunch (Wi-Fi woke up), all behind the old spurt's clock. The first one ends the old spurt, the rest queue; the spurt-start rule then keeps the newest target's worth. No underrun, no target change.

cases.name: late packets with contiguous ts
cases._why: The network delay grows by 60 ms mid-spurt. Without a ts jump it is an underrun: seq 10 arrives after its slot and is dropped (target + 20 ms). Seq 11 is late as well, but by then its ts is two frames past the last played one and the only seq between is the late seq 10, so it starts a new spurt at the raised target.

cases.name: re-anchor
cases._why: The output takes 8 extra frames at once at 300 ms (a route switch), so the playout clock runs ahead of the stream, and seq 15 is lost. Every later packet is late and, with the real seq gap, cannot be a new spurt: underruns (one raise) until the late run has lasted 100 ms with nothing played, then the next late packet (seq 21) starts a new spurt.

cases.name: seq and ts wrap-around
cases._why: seq passes 65535 and ts passes 2^32 mid-spurt; one frame lost right after the wrap is decoded with FEC, a silence gap with a keepalive follows.

cases.name: sender restart
cases._why: A ts more than 3 s away from the playout clock: everything queued is dropped and the buffer starts over (new spurt, same target), whatever the seq.

cases.name: late burst after a network stall
cases._why: Nothing arrives for 200 ms mid-spurt, then the 10 missing frames at once. The first is an underrun; the second starts a new spurt at the raised target (its ts is two frames past the last played one, the seq between came late), and the spurt-start rule keeps the newest 60 ms.
